newsitem.title: USA: Group buys stake in Brazil power firm for $1.1 billion.
newsitem.headline: Group buys stake in Brazil power firm for $1.1 billion.

text.p: A group led by U.S.-based AES Corp. and a unit of Atlanta-based Southern Co. bought a 33 percent stake in the Brazilian power company Cemig for about $1.1 billion, officials said Wednesday.
Industry analysts said that a stagnant U.S. market is forcing the nation's power companies to try to beef up their earnings overseas but the potential rewards are matched by risks.
"Returns in the U.S. are low and the market is so regulated that even the worst conditions overseas are better than here," said Edward Tirello, an analyst for NatWest Securities.

Cemig is the latest deal in a series for both Southern and AES and comes just a week after Southern and Germany's Veba AG announced they would pay $1.9 billion for a stake in Berliner Kraft und Licht AG, the biggest electricity supplier in Berlin.
Southern's core business is growing at just 2 to 2-1/2 percent a year.

"We aim to have 30 percent of our business outside our traditional business, and while some will be in domestic energy marketing, a significant part of that will be overseas," said Southern spokesman Chuck Griffin.
Stock exchange officials in Brazil said five groups had pre-qualified to bid on Cemig bonds, which are convertible to common shares at the Rio de Janeiro Stock Exchange.
But only the AES/Southern Electric group entered a bid for the state-owned firm. The gavel came down on the sale moments after the auction started.
It was Southern's first acquisition in the Brazilian electricity sector. AES already owns a stake in Rio de Janeiro power company Light, which was privatised last year.

"We view this association with much expectation for growth," said Luiz David Travesso, AES vice-president in Brazil. "Cemig is in a position to expand its activities and its generating capacity within the state and within the country."
Southern's return on its core business is 12 to 13 percent and it is looking for more than that, noting the Brazilian deal would be "immediately beneficial to earnings."
The consortium, which also includes a group of funds formed by Brazilian bank Opportunity, said the company has the potential to expand its operations to other areas of Brazil.
Not all U.S. companies are long-term players overseas, some are just using non-U.S. markets as a shelter while the American regulatory mess is cleared up.
"The big players in the overseas market such as Southern, Duke Power Co. and CMS Energy Corp. all go in with local partners and just get going," said Tirello.

For independent power producer AES, the latest deal is the third in the target of 10 project wins the company set itself for 1997 and maintains the company's focus on Latin America, especially Brazil where it owns a stake in neighbouring utility Light Servicos de Eletricidade SA.
AES stock fell $2.25 to $69.875 while Southern Co. rose 25 cents to $21.50, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
